title: Sharks can hear sounds from nearly 250 feet away
summary:
The ocean is full of sound. Scientists wanted to know how far a shark swimming freely in the ocean can hear, and whether it can tell where a faraway sound comes from. A new study from Florida Atlantic University begins to answer those questions.

The researchers studied blacktip sharks in shallow coastal waters off Palm Beach County in Florida. Large numbers of these sharks gather there each winter, and the clear water let scientists watch them from above. The team placed an underwater speaker in the water. It drifted with the current as far as 19 meters from their boat. They played three groups of low-frequency sounds. They also played a control sound, which is a sound used for comparison, and it was higher than sharks are known to hear. A drone flying 40 to 50 meters above the water recorded how the sharks moved.

The sharks reacted to all three low-frequency sounds but not to the control sound. They detected the low sounds from up to 74 meters (243 feet) away. That is farther than had been shown before in free-swimming sharks. The sharks also often made quick turns away from the speaker. That means they could tell which direction the sound came from.

Sharks do not have a gas-filled swim bladder like many bony fish. Scientists believe sharks mostly use their inner ears. One part is called the macula neglecta, which may help them sense vibrations as sound travels through water. The study was published in Integrative Organismal Biology.
why_it_matters: Sharks sense the world in ways people do not fully understand. Learning how they hear can help scientists understand how they find food and avoid danger.
